Today, many companies use special software to check how hard their workers are working, for example by counting their keyboard use or taking screenshots of their computer. In my opinion, this is a negative development, although it has a few advantages for employers.

On the one hand, managers say that this software help them to make the company more efficient. They can see which employees are working hard and which are wasting time on social media. This information can be used to give rewards to good workers. Also, when people work from home, the manager cannot see them, so the software is the only way to check that they are doing their job.

On the other hand, I believe the disadvantages are much bigger. The first problem is that employees feel stressful when they know that a computer is watching them all the time. They may be afraid to take a short break or talk with colleagues, even though these things are normal and can help them to work better. As a result, their mental health can become worse.

The second problem is that the software does not measure real productivity. For instance, a designer who spend an hour thinking about a new idea may look lazy to the program, because he does not type anything. On the other hand, a worker who moves the mouse all day may look busy but produce nothing useful. So the company can make wrong decisions about their staff.

In conclusion, I think using software to monitor employees is a negative development because it creates stress and it cannot measure the quality of work properly. Companies should trust their staff more and judge them by the result of their work.

samples.text:
With the growth of remote working, a rising number of employers have begun using software that records how long staff spend on particular tasks, which websites they visit and even how often they type. Although this technology may seem to offer greater efficiency, I believe it is essentially a negative development.

Supporters argue that monitoring tools give managers useful information. When teams work from home, it can be difficult to know whether tasks are being completed, and data on working patterns may help identify employees who are struggling or processes that waste time. Some also claim that such software is fair, since it judges everyone by the same objective standard.

However, the main weakness of this approach is that activity is not the same as productivity. Software can count keystrokes and log screen time, but it cannot measure the quality of a report, the value of a creative idea or the time an employee spends helping a colleague. As a result, workers may learn to appear busy rather than to work well, for example by keeping their mouse moving or avoiding tasks that involve thinking away from the computer.

Perhaps more importantly, constant surveillance damages trust between staff and management. Employees who feel watched every minute are likely to experience higher levels of stress, and many will feel that their employer does not respect them as professionals. This can lower morale and, ironically, lead to lower productivity and higher staff turnover. There is also a risk that personal data collected in this way are misused.

In conclusion, while monitoring software may give employers a sense of control, it measures the wrong things and undermines the trust on which good workplaces depend. For these reasons, I consider its increasing use to be a negative trend.
samples.why: Clear position maintained · counter-argument presented then rebutted with extended reasoning · logical progression and varied cohesion · good vocabulary (staff turnover, morale) · frequent error-free sentences.

samples.text:
Software that logs keystrokes, captures screenshots and scores employees on their apparent activity has spread rapidly, particularly since remote work became widespread. Employers present it as a neutral tool for improving efficiency, but I would argue that its growing use is, on the whole, a negative development.

It is not difficult to see why managers find such tools attractive. Supervising a dispersed workforce is genuinely challenging, and aggregated data can reveal bottlenecks, uneven workloads or employees who may need additional support. In highly routine roles, such as processing claims or answering calls, some measurement of output is both reasonable and long established.

The central flaw, however, is that these programs mistake visible activity for valuable work. Much of what makes an employee effective, whether analysing a problem, mentoring a junior colleague or simply thinking before acting, leaves little digital trace. A system that rewards constant typing and penalises periods of inactivity therefore encourages staff to perform busyness rather than to achieve results, and may even discourage the reflective work on which innovation depends. In this sense, monitoring can distort the very productivity it claims to measure.

Equally damaging is its effect on the relationship between employer and employee. Continuous surveillance communicates distrust, and people who feel perpetually observed tend to become anxious, less willing to take initiative and more inclined to leave. Talented staff, who have the greatest choice of employers, are often the first to go. Furthermore, the detailed personal data such systems accumulate create obvious risks if they are stored carelessly or used for purposes employees never agreed to.

In conclusion, although monitoring software can offer useful insights in certain narrowly defined roles, its widespread use rests on a flawed understanding of what productive work looks like and erodes workplace trust. Organisations would be better served by judging employees on the outcomes they deliver.
samples.why: Clear, nuanced negative judgement · concession handled precisely · ideas developed with insightful reasoning · sophisticated cohesion and paragraphing · wide, precise vocabulary (perform busyness, erodes) · error-free complex structures.
